title: Ibrahim, an example
hookLine: in Ibrahim and those with him is an excellent example (60:4)
tomorrow: Kindness to those who don't fight you

cards: An excellent example. In Surah Al-Ahzab, the Qur'an uses that phrase for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In Surah sixty it uses it again, this time for Ibrahim, Abraham, the friend of God, and those who stood beside him.
Being named an example is a heavy honor. People are meant to copy you, and copying is never abstract: it's how you speak, who you stand up to, who you feed.
Surah sixty shows two sides of Ibrahim at once, and quietly marks one thing not to copy.

teach.b: Verse four. Pickthall: "There is a goodly pattern for you in Abraham and those with him". The Arabic is uswa hasana, an excellent example, the same phrase Al-Ahzab uses for the Prophet.
Then the verse says what the pattern is.
Ibrahim and those with him told their own people, plainly, that they would not worship what their people worshipped besides God. They stood firm, even against their own families. That's one side.
The surah, named for a woman who is tested, was revealed at a time of divided loyalties, and it speaks to people torn between faith and family.
But the same verse makes one exception: Ibrahim's words to his father, I will ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to do anything for you against God.

The verse sets that promise outside the pattern, and Surah At-Tawbah says Ibrahim later stopped asking forgiveness for his father, once it was clear his father was an enemy to God. Still, the way he spoke is remembered.
Surah Maryam keeps the moment: Ibrahim says to his father, peace be upon you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Firm in belief, gentle in speech. That's the second side.
And elsewhere the Qur'an shows a third: his table. In Surah Adh-Dhariyat, strangers arrive at Ibrahim's door. He doesn't know who they are.
He hurries to his family and comes back with a fattened calf. Firm, tender, and quick to feed a stranger. The verse calls the whole pattern beautiful.

how: Muslims honor Ibrahim as the friend of God, khalil Allah, and invoke him in every prayer; his hospitality is held up as a model, and Muslim hosts often speak of honoring the guest as a duty of faith.

o: the prophet who first received the Qur'an in Mecca
the prophet whose staff turned into a serpent
the friend of God, held up as a pattern to follow

games.q: Ibrahim as an example — tap the pairs.
p: uses the phrase for the Prophet

s: the Qur'an uses 'an excellent example' for Ibrahim and for the Prophet Muhammad
Surah sixty for Ibrahim, Al-Ahzab for the Prophet.
Ibrahim spoke harshly to his father when they parted
he said peace be upon you and promised to ask forgiveness for him.
Ibrahim knew his guests were angels before he served them
he didn't know them, and hurried to bring a fattened calf.

games.q: strangers arrive at Ibrahim's door. he doesn't know who they are. what does he do?
o: asks who they are before letting them in.
hurries to his family and brings a fattened calf.
offers them water and sends them on.
games.why: he brought the best he had, before even knowing who they were.

practice: Picture your own door, desk or table, and who might come to it this week: a neighbor, a new colleague, a friend you've lost touch with. Picture Ibrahim hurrying to bring the best he had.
Choose one small act of welcome you could offer, a cup of tea, a seat, a warm hello, and hold it in mind.

wordCard.voice: Ibrahim. In him and those with him, Surah sixty says, is an excellent example: firm in faith, tender with his father, generous at his table. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: an excellent example, a beautiful pattern. Used for Ibrahim (60:4, 60:6) and the Prophet (33:21).

carryVoice: Your line: an excellent example. Firm, tender and generous, all in one person. Until tomorrow.
